group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man arrived this morning to the pre-operative assessment unit for medical optimization before an elective posterolateral thoracotomy with left upper lobectomy and mediastinal lymph node dissection planned in four days for biopsy-proven stage IA2 adenocarcinoma; the thoracic surgical team anticipates a four-hour intrathoracic exposure, single-lung ventilation, and anticipated blood loss approaching 500 mL, with admission to the cardiothoracic step-down unit post-procedure. He reports that over the past month he has continued his usual activities—painting the porch, walking his dog briskly for 20 minutes twice daily, and carrying groceries up one flight—without dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal breathing disturbances, ankle swelling, or unexpected weight gain. Twice weekly he climbs three flights of stadium stairs to watch his grandson’s baseball games, stopping once to catch his breath more from deconditioning than chest pressure. Six years ago he experienced a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction while shoveling snow; emergent coronary angiography revealed a 95 % proximal right coronary artery lesion, successfully treated with a drug-eluting stent. He completed cardiac rehabilitation and has been free of recurrent angina, emergency department visits, or additional revascularization. Follow-up transthoracic echocardiography obtained last winter for an insurance physical documented a left ventricular ejection fraction of 58 % with normal wall motion and no structural abnormalities. He takes metoprolol succinate 50 mg every morning and aspirin 81 mg daily; prasugrel was discontinued by his cardiologist three years post-stent, and he has remained symptom-free since. Additional chronic illnesses include well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed exclusively with lifestyle measures and metformin 1000 mg twice daily—he has never required injectable glucose-lowering agents—essential hypertension on lisinopril 20 mg nightly, and mixed dyslipidemia treated with high-intensity rosuvastatin 40 mg. There is no personal history of cerebrovascular accident, transient neurologic deficit, peripheral arterial intervention, chronic lung disease beyond mild seasonal allergic rhinitis, or renal colic. He quit cigarette smoking immediately after his infarction (20 pack-years) and limits alcohol to one glass of red wine on weekends; he denies illicit drug use. Family history is notable for a father who died of a large anterior myocardial infarction at age 62 and a mother living with osteoarthritis into her late eighties. Allergies consist of urticaria with ampicillin. On examination he appears fit, conversant, and euvolemic. Temperature is 36.6 °C, blood pressure 126/74 mm Hg in the right arm seated, heart rate 64 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Neck veins are not distended; carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit. Cardiac auscultation reveals a crisp S1 and S2, no gallops, rubs, or murmurs. Lungs demonstrate vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with faint wheeze at the left apex but no crackles. Abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Extremities show no edema; dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ and symmetric. Neurologic exam reveals full strength and normal sensation in all limbs. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn an hour before the visit reveal hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 218 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, consistent with prior baselines; estimated glomerular filtration rate is 67 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting glucose measured simultaneously is 118 mg/dL, and a glycated hemoglobin from last month was 6.8 %. Coagulation profile shows an INR 1.0 and aPTT within reference range. Resting 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 62 bpm, Q-waves in the inferior leads compatible with his old infarct, and no acute ST-T changes. A recent pulmonary function test performed by pulmonology for operative planning shows FEV₁ 81 % predicted and DLCO 76 % predicted, deemed adequate for planned resection. Chest imaging has already been reviewed by thoracic surgery, revealing no contralateral disease and stable cardiac silhouette. He has been instructed to continue his beta-blocker, statin, and metformin up to the evening before surgery, hold aspirin only on the morning of the procedure per anesthesiology preference, remain nil per os after midnight, and arrive two hours prior to scheduled incision for arterial line placement and epidural analgesia.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative criteria:
- High-risk surgery: the planned thoracotomy with lobectomy is intrathoracic surgery → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: prior NSTEMI qualifies despite successful stenting and no current angina → 1.
- History of heart failure: none reported → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: diabetes is managed with metformin and lifestyle measures, not insulin → 0.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
